A shared gradient is a constraint on the examples that generated it. Conceptually, an observer could seek candidate inputs whose model gradients match the observed update, making small batches and informative early layers especially concerning. This explains why “raw data never leaves the device” is not a complete privacy claim. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.00133) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.05629)

Defenses include secure aggregation over sufficiently many clients, clipping plus calibrated differential-privacy noise, reduced update exposure, and strict authorization/retention controls. Aggregation hides individual updates under its threat assumptions; DP bounds participation-dependent information under its accountant. Evaluate leakage in an authorized test environment across batch sizes and adversary knowledge. Compression or larger batches may complicate reconstruction but should not be represented as formal privacy guarantees.
